title: One Online Order
subtitle: Buy Now to the doorstep
learningObjective: Map the process, find the decisions, judge whether AI fits, and design only the decisions that survive.
throughline: Hunt for the diamonds — that is where AI replaces judgment.

introduction.title: What happens after a customer selects Buy Now?
introduction.context: An online order looks like one transaction to the customer, but fulfilling it crosses commerce, fraud operations, warehouse, carrier, and support teams. Each handoff can change whether the order is accepted, where inventory is sourced, what delivery promise is made, and how an exception is resolved.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one order through address and payment checks, inventory and carrier assignment, picking and packing, delivery monitoring, and customer support. The exception paths reveal the manual review, oversold inventory, late-delivery, and remedy work hidden behind the normal path.
introduction.startsWhen: The customer submits items, delivery details, payment, and account context.
introduction.endsWhen: The order is delivered and kept, or its final exception and remedy are resolved.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Items, address, card, account history

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Verify, allocate stock, pick, pack, label

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Is this payment good? Which carrier?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Ship, hold for review, or cancel

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: It arrived Thursday, and they kept it

decisions.label: Is this address deliverable?
decisions.wrongCost: A parcel goes nowhere
decisions.testAnswer: No. Another year of data does not change a published postal rule.
decisions.why: The format and service-area logic are stable and known in advance.
decisions.recommendation: Implement deterministic validation and address correction, not a model.

decisions.label: Is this payment fraudulent?
decisions.wrongCost: A chargeback, or a good customer lost
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. New outcomes reveal changing fraud patterns that nobody has fully written down.
decisions.why: The decision depends on patterns across many prior examples and changes as fraud tactics move.
decisions.recommendation: Rank payments into approve, review, and decline buckets; route ambiguity to an analyst.

data.summary: Three years of orders and final outcomes, not only analyst approvals.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: owned, labelled, refreshing
data.risk: Historical labels record what analysts decided, not necessarily what was true.

method.output: Approve, review, or decline
method.technique: Explainable gradient-boosted classifier on tabular features

metric.technical: Catch 85% of currently detected fraud while sending under 3% of good orders to review.
metric.business: Halve 83 monthly review hours without increasing chargebacks or rejecting good customers.
metric.baseline: 40,000 orders × 3.1% flagged × 4 minutes = 83 staff-hours per month

human.checkpoint: Review genuinely ambiguous payments with evidence and enough time to decide.
human.falsePositiveCost: A legitimate customer is blocked and may not return.
human.falseNegativeCost: Fraud succeeds; the retailer loses goods, payment, and a chargeback fee.

decisions.label: Will it arrive when promised?
decisions.wrongCost: A broken promise and a support ticket
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Weather, seasonal volume, route, and carrier performance change with new data.
decisions.why: The outcome is uncertain and must be estimated from historical delivery results.
decisions.recommendation: Predict the probability or expected delay, then surface risk before promising a date.

data.summary: Historical promised and actual delivery times joined to route conditions.
data.readiness: Cross-team data; expect ownership and integration work
data.risk: Averages hide the expensive late tail; actual outcomes must be captured consistently.

method.output: Expected arrival or probability of missing the promise
method.technique: Supervised delivery-time prediction with calibrated uncertainty

metric.technical: MAE or RMSE in delivery days, plus performance on the worst 5% of misses.
metric.business: Reduce broken promises and related support tickets from the 1.8% late baseline.
metric.baseline: 1.8% of orders delivered late under the synthetic baseline

human.checkpoint: Set acceptable risk thresholds and review persistent carrier or route failures.
human.falsePositiveCost: An unnecessarily conservative promise may reduce conversion.
human.falseNegativeCost: A confident but late promise creates support cost and lost trust.

decisions.label: Which warehouse, which carrier?
decisions.wrongCost: Extra freight cost, or a late delivery
decisions.testAnswer: No training data is required if the objective and constraints can be written exactly.
decisions.why: This is an assignment problem with costs, capacity, inventory, service levels, and routes.
decisions.recommendation: Use an operations-research solver before considering machine learning.

decisions.label: What do we tell an unhappy customer?
decisions.wrongCost: Churn, or a refund the retailer never owed
decisions.testAnswer: The policy decision stays separate; generation can draft the communication from grounded facts.
decisions.why: Generation produces an artifact inside a process box rather than resolving the policy diamond.
decisions.recommendation: Ground a draft in actual order status and policy, then require agent review before sending.

data.summary: Current order, tracking events, approved policy, prior contact, and tone guidance.
data.readiness: Operational sources exist but must be joined and permissioned
data.risk: A fluent draft can still invent status, policy, or compensation.

method.output: A grounded draft response
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded text generation with policy and order tools

metric.technical: Groundedness and unsupported-claim rate.
metric.business: Human acceptance rate, response time, repeat contacts, and avoidable refunds.
metric.baseline: About 900 monthly support cases in the synthetic baseline

human.checkpoint: Verify facts, policy, tone, and remedy before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The system offers compensation or makes a promise that policy does not support.
human.falseNegativeCost: The response omits a real issue and the customer contacts support again.

decisions.label: Refund, replace, or deny?
decisions.wrongCost: Margin, or a customer who never returns
decisions.testAnswer: The costs are lopsided and the judgment combines policy, context, and customer impact.
decisions.why: A model can prepare evidence, but it should not own the consequential remedy decision in this first design.
decisions.recommendation: Improve the evidence shown to the support lead; keep final authority with the human.

title: One Card Transaction
subtitle: From authorization request to accountable fraud outcome
learningObjective: Map payment screening as an operating process, separate the learned classification from policy routing, and preserve human authority over fraud determination.
throughline: The model prioritizes review; policy routes work; a human determines fraud.

introduction.title: What happens between a card purchase and a fraud outcome?
introduction.context: A fraud score is only one signal inside a payment-screening process. A transaction must be validated, represented with point-in-time information, scored, tested against an operating cutoff, and sometimes investigated before anyone can determine whether fraud occurred.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one card transaction through request validation, known-block checks, point-in-time feature preparation, random-forest classification, cutoff policy, authorization, analyst review, evidence collection, and outcome recording. Exception paths reveal the correction and investigation work hidden behind the normal authorization path.
introduction.startsWhen: A cardholder submits a purchase and the payment gateway receives an authorization request.
introduction.endsWhen: The transaction continues as normal or a fraud analyst records an evidence-supported case outcome.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Purchase, merchant, time, location, prior card activity

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Validate, engineer features, score, investigate

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Valid? Known block? Review? Fraud occurred?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Continue authorization, correct, queue, or intervene

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Normal transaction or confirmed fraud outcome

baseline.label: known fraud caught
baseline.note: Recall on the held-out future period

baseline.label: reviewed alerts confirmed fraud
baseline.note: Precision in the held-out review queue

decisions.label: Is the authorization request structurally valid?
decisions.wrongCost: A malformed request enters scoring, or a valid purchase is rejected before screening
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required fields, formats, ranges, and timestamps are explicit interface requirements.
decisions.why: The validity conditions are known in advance and should behave consistently without learning from outcomes.
decisions.recommendation: Apply deterministic schema, range, timestamp, and required-field validation before feature engineering.

decisions.label: Is the card, account, or merchant on a known block list?
decisions.wrongCost: A known threat continues, or stale policy blocks a legitimate purchase
decisions.testAnswer: No. An exact match against an approved, current list is deterministic policy logic.
decisions.why: Known blocks should remain explicit, versioned, and auditable rather than hidden inside model behavior.
decisions.recommendation: Use versioned exact-match rules with ownership, expiration, and an exception path for disputed entries.

decisions.label: Does this transaction resemble known fraud patterns?
decisions.frequency: Every transaction that passes deterministic checks
decisions.wrongCost: Fraud is missed, or a normal transaction consumes scarce analyst capacity
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Confirmed outcomes reveal changing combinations of amount, velocity, merchant, time, location, and customer context.
decisions.why: The relationship between point-in-time transaction context and later fraud outcomes is learned from labeled examples rather than fully written as rules.
decisions.recommendation: Produce an uncalibrated ranking score, then keep the review cutoff and final fraud determination outside the model.

data.summary: Synthetic card transactions joined to merchant context, prior card activity, customer context, and confirmed historical outcomes.
data.owner: Payment data platform and fraud operations
data.readiness: Prepared point-in-time features with an earlier training window and later held-out test period
data.risk: Historical labels arrive after the decision and may reflect investigation coverage; feature generation must exclude future information.

method.output: An uncalibrated ranking score used to prioritize review
method.technique: Random forest with random undersampling, packaged as an MLflow pyfunc

metric.technical: 91.1% recall and 18.7% precision at a fixed 3% review budget on the held-out future period.
metric.business: Catch most known fraud while limiting the queue to the analyst capacity represented by the 3% review budget.
metric.baseline: A 72.9% ranking-score cutoff routes 25 prepared held-out transactions to review

human.checkpoint: Investigate evidence for prioritized transactions and record the final case outcome.
human.falsePositiveCost: A normal transaction consumes analyst time and may delay or inconvenience the cardholder.
human.falseNegativeCost: Fraud continues and can create financial loss, recovery work, and customer harm.

decisions.label: Is the ranking score at or above the review cutoff?
decisions.wrongCost: The queue exceeds capacity, or high-ranked fraud is allowed to pass without review
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the score and approved cutoff are available, the branch is a deterministic comparison.
decisions.why: The model estimates rank; the 3% capacity constraint determines policy. Keeping them separate makes workload choices visible.
decisions.recommendation: Version the cutoff, record which policy routed each transaction, and monitor queue volume and outcomes.

decisions.label: Is the required investigation evidence available?
decisions.wrongCost: An analyst decides from incomplete context, or a resolvable case waits unnecessarily
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required artifacts, access checks, freshness windows, and retrieval status can be stated explicitly.
decisions.why: The system can assemble and verify the investigation packet without deciding what the evidence means.
decisions.recommendation: Use deterministic completeness and freshness checks, then expose missing evidence rather than silently filling gaps.

decisions.label: Did fraud occur?
decisions.wrongCost: A legitimate customer is treated as fraudulent, or actual fraud remains unresolved
decisions.testAnswer: The ranking score is not proof. Final disposition depends on evidence, policy, customer context, and accountable judgment.
decisions.why: This consequential decision creates the operational outcome and future training label; the reviewer must be able to challenge the model.
decisions.recommendation: Present source evidence and model context, require an analyst disposition, and preserve appeal and correction paths.

title: One Equipment Alert
subtitle: From noisy signal to safe return to service
learningObjective: Separate signal validation, failure prediction, inspection prioritization, diagnostic support, and accountable equipment action.
throughline: A risk score can focus attention; it cannot authorize a shutdown.

introduction.title: Why one machine alert becomes a cross-team decision
introduction.context: Industrial equipment produces a steady stream of alarms and sensor readings, but many alerts are duplicates, noise, or signs that do not require immediate intervention. Reliability and maintenance teams must identify real failure risk, use scarce technicians and parts well, and protect production without allowing a prediction to control equipment directly.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one alert through signal validation, asset-history enrichment, 48-hour failure-risk estimation, inspection prioritization, work-order creation, field diagnosis, and an accountable decision to monitor, repair, run at reduced output, or stop the equipment.
introduction.startsWhen: A monitored machine produces an alert that may indicate changing equipment condition.
introduction.endsWhen: The alert is closed as noise, the asset remains under monitoring, or repair is verified and the asset is safe to operate.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Telemetry, asset history, operating context

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Validate, enrich, triage, inspect

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Failure risk? Inspect first? Stop equipment?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Monitor, diagnose, repair, or shut down

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Safe availability with fewer surprise stops

decisions.label: Is this signal valid?
decisions.wrongCost: Wasted inspection capacity, or a real warning discarded
decisions.testAnswer: No. Range checks, stale timestamps, duplicate windows, and sensor-health flags are known validation logic.
decisions.why: The cheapest first step is deterministic validation before any learned pattern is trusted.
decisions.recommendation: Apply sensor-health, freshness, range, and duplicate-event rules; route unresolved quality failures for instrumentation repair.

decisions.label: Will this asset fail within 48 hours?
decisions.wrongCost: An unnecessary interruption, or an unplanned production stop
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Confirmed outcomes reveal changing combinations of vibration, temperature, load, and prior repair history.
decisions.why: The output is the calibrated probability of a future event over a defined time horizon.
decisions.recommendation: Estimate 48-hour failure risk with uncertainty and evidence; never connect the score directly to equipment control.

data.summary: Time-aligned telemetry joined to asset configuration, maintenance actions, and confirmed failure outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: 18 months available; failure labels require review
data.risk: Work orders record what technicians did, not always the true failure mode; leakage from post-failure signals can inflate results.

method.output: Probability of confirmed failure within 48 hours
method.technique: Calibrated supervised prediction over engineered time-window features

metric.technical: Calibration error and recall at the inspection-capacity threshold, segmented by asset class.
metric.business: Increase useful inspections and reduce the six monthly unplanned stops without increasing unnecessary shutdowns.
metric.baseline: 1,800 alerts, 140 inspections, and 6 unplanned stops per month

human.checkpoint: Review evidence, uncertainty, operating context, and recent maintenance before recommending action.
human.falsePositiveCost: A healthy asset consumes scarce inspection time or is interrupted unnecessarily.
human.falseNegativeCost: A failure is missed and causes safety exposure, downtime, or secondary damage.

decisions.label: Which asset should be inspected first?
decisions.wrongCost: A high-impact asset waits while capacity is spent elsewhere
decisions.testAnswer: The inputs may include predictions, but the choice is an allocation problem with technicians, parts, access windows, and production impact.
decisions.why: A stated objective and explicit constraints are more transparent than asking a model to imitate historical schedules.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize the inspection queue using risk, consequence, capacity, access, skills, and parts constraints.

decisions.label: Should a work order be opened?
decisions.wrongCost: Duplicate work and queue noise, or an approved task never reaches a technician
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once required evidence, priority, and duplicate checks pass, the handoff is deterministic.
decisions.why: This is controlled workflow automation, not a judgment that improves by learning from examples.
decisions.recommendation: Create a work order only after required fields, duplicate, authorization, and scheduling checks pass.

decisions.label: What should the technician check next?
decisions.wrongCost: Longer diagnosis, an unsafe instruction, or a missed root cause
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can assemble a context-specific diagnostic brief, but the technician must validate it against the asset and safety procedure.
decisions.why: The output is a grounded work artifact, not the final equipment decision.
decisions.recommendation: Draft evidence-linked checks from current signals, manuals, prior repairs, and approved procedures for technician review.

data.summary: Current alert evidence, asset manual, approved safety procedures, prior work orders, and known-failure guidance.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: manuals are approved; work-order notes vary in quality
data.risk: A fluent diagnostic sequence can omit lockout requirements or repeat an incorrect historical repair.

method.output: Evidence-linked diagnostic brief and suggested check sequence
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation with asset, procedure, and work-history tools

metric.technical: Grounded claim rate, required-safety-step coverage, and unsupported-instruction rate.
metric.business: Reduce first-diagnosis time and repeat visits without increasing safety deviations or unnecessary parts use.
metric.baseline: 140 monthly inspections with technician review required for every brief

human.checkpoint: Confirm asset identity, lockout requirements, observed condition, and each diagnostic action before execution.
human.falsePositiveCost: The technician performs an irrelevant or disruptive check.
human.falseNegativeCost: The brief omits a critical cause or safety step and the asset returns to service incorrectly.

decisions.label: Should operations stop the equipment?
decisions.frequency: Only when evidence indicates consequential risk
decisions.wrongCost: Production is interrupted unnecessarily, or unsafe equipment continues running
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own this consequential action. The decision combines evidence, safety procedure, production state, and accountable authority.
decisions.why: Predictions and diagnostic evidence inform the decision, but they do not carry operational accountability.
decisions.recommendation: Present evidence and escalation criteria; require an authorized supervisor to stop, derate, or continue operation.

title: One Customer Identity (KYC) Review
subtitle: From customer submission to accountable case disposition
learningObjective: Separate document interpretation, explicit policy checks, screening triage, workflow automation, and accountable compliance judgment.
throughline: AI can prepare and triage evidence; policy stays explicit and disposition stays human.

introduction.title: What a customer identity review is protecting
introduction.context: Know Your Customer, or KYC, is the regulated process used to verify who a customer is, understand beneficial ownership, and identify evidence that requires additional review before an account is opened. The work combines variable documents with explicit policy, screening requirements, and decisions that can materially affect both the institution and the applicant.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one onboarding packet through document extraction, identity and ownership normalization, completeness and consistency checks, approved screening, review routing, and human disposition. Low-confidence evidence, missing documents, conflicting records, and uncertain screening matches create the exception paths.
introduction.startsWhen: An applicant submits identity, onboarding, and ownership evidence.
introduction.endsWhen: An authorized compliance role records a clear, escalate, or decline disposition with supporting evidence.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Identity documents, forms, ownership, policy

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Intake, extract, normalize, screen

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Reliable? Complete? Consistent? Potential match?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Clear, request evidence, or escalate

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Traceable analyst-owned disposition

decisions.label: Can the required evidence be extracted reliably?
decisions.wrongCost: Bad fields contaminate every later check, or a readable packet is delayed
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Document layouts, image quality, and field representations vary, and reviewed examples improve extraction confidence and document classification.
decisions.why: The system must classify document and field evidence while exposing uncertainty and source location.
decisions.recommendation: Extract field values with source citations and confidence; send low-confidence evidence to document review.

data.summary: Representative onboarding documents paired with reviewed field values, document classes, and extraction outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: approved sample set exists; rare layouts need coverage review
data.risk: Historical reviewer corrections may be inconsistent, and aggregate accuracy can hide weak performance on rare documents.

method.output: Document class, field values, source citations, and confidence
method.technique: Layout-aware document extraction with field-level confidence and abstention

metric.technical: Field precision, field recall, packet classification accuracy, and grounded citation rate by document type.
metric.business: Reduce 360 monthly preparation hours while keeping exception rework and incorrect straight-through packets below baseline.
metric.baseline: 5,000 packets with 24% entering 18 minutes of exception preparation

human.checkpoint: Verify low-confidence values against the source image and record corrections without deciding customer disposition.
human.falsePositiveCost: An incorrect field is treated as reliable and contaminates policy or screening checks.
human.falseNegativeCost: Usable evidence is rejected and creates avoidable applicant and analyst work.

decisions.label: Are all policy-required fields present?
decisions.wrongCost: An incomplete case advances, or an applicant is asked for evidence that is not required
decisions.testAnswer: No. Versioned policy defines required documents and fields for each product, entity type, and jurisdiction.
decisions.why: Explicit policy checks are more transparent and auditable than learning requirements from historical analyst behavior.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate versioned completeness rules and identify every missing requirement with its policy source.

decisions.label: Do identity and ownership records agree?
decisions.wrongCost: A material conflict is missed, or harmless formatting differences create rework
decisions.testAnswer: Mostly no. Exact comparison, approved normalization, date tolerance, and ownership-total rules resolve the known cases; ambiguity should be escalated.
decisions.why: Known consistency checks should remain deterministic and explainable at field level.
decisions.recommendation: Normalize approved variants, apply explicit comparisons and tolerances, and escalate unresolved source conflicts.

decisions.label: Is this a plausible screening match?
decisions.wrongCost: A real risk is missed, or a customer is delayed by a false match
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Reviewed outcomes improve ranking across names, aliases, dates, jurisdictions, and incomplete identifiers, but uncertainty must be visible.
decisions.why: The output is a present-state match class, not a final compliance decision.
decisions.recommendation: Rank candidate matches as likely, uncertain, or unlikely with field-level comparison evidence for analyst review.

data.summary: Approved screening lists, normalized applicant identifiers, candidate pairs, and analyst-confirmed match outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: list provenance is controlled and reviewed match outcomes are retained
data.risk: Name and geography patterns can create unequal false-positive burdens; list freshness and identity resolution are critical.

method.output: Likely match, uncertain match, or unlikely match with comparison evidence
method.technique: High-recall candidate generation followed by calibrated pair classification

metric.technical: Recall of confirmed matches, false-positive rate, calibration, and subgroup review burden.
metric.business: Reduce avoidable screening review time without increasing missed confirmed matches or customer delay.
metric.baseline: All potential matches require analyst disposition under the defined review boundary

human.checkpoint: Compare source records, resolve uncertain identity evidence, and document the match rationale.
human.falsePositiveCost: A customer experiences unnecessary delay, investigation, or adverse treatment.
human.falseNegativeCost: A material screening match is missed and the institution accepts unmanaged risk.

decisions.label: Which approved review queue receives the packet?
decisions.wrongCost: A case waits in the wrong queue or bypasses required specialist review
decisions.testAnswer: No. Product, jurisdiction, issue type, risk flags, and required reviewer role define an auditable routing table.
decisions.why: Once evidence and statuses are established, queue routing is controlled execution rather than learned judgment.
decisions.recommendation: Route through versioned mappings and fail closed when no authorized destination exists.

decisions.label: Should this case be cleared, escalated, or declined?
decisions.wrongCost: The institution accepts unmanaged risk, or a customer receives an unjustified adverse outcome
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own regulated case disposition. Evidence, policy, uncertainty, customer impact, and accountable authority must remain visible.
decisions.why: AI and rules prepare the packet; an authorized officer owns the consequential conclusion and rationale.
decisions.recommendation: Require human disposition with cited evidence, policy version, conflict history, and an auditable rationale.

title: One Resident Service Request
subtitle: From everyday language to the right accountable service
learningObjective: Separate language interpretation, entitlement rules, capacity allocation, grounded communication, and accountable exception handling.
throughline: Use AI for language ambiguity, rules for entitlement, and people for accountable exceptions.

introduction.title: Why a simple resident request can be difficult to route
introduction.context: Residents describe needs in everyday language, while public services are organized by program, jurisdiction, eligibility, and provider capacity. They also carry safeguarding duties: responding quickly when a person may be at risk of harm. A wrong first route makes people repeat their story, delays support, and can hide an urgent situation that needs trained human attention.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one request from natural-language intake through service classification, jurisdiction and eligibility checks, duplicate handling, provider assignment, resident communication, and exception review. Clarification, transfers, capacity limits, and urgent protection escalation form the main alternate paths.
introduction.startsWhen: A resident submits a request through an available intake channel.
introduction.endsWhen: The appropriate service receives a routed case with verified context, or an urgent exception is escalated and recorded.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Resident request, location, service catalog

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Interpret, verify, match, route

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Which need? Eligible? Which office? Exception?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Clarify, assign, escalate, or create case

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Resident reaches the right service with context

decisions.label: Which service need is the resident describing?
decisions.wrongCost: The resident repeats their story, loses time, or never reaches the right service
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Reviewed requests reveal varied language, multilingual phrasing, and overlapping descriptions that improve service-category matching.
decisions.why: The output is a present-state service category with confidence, not an entitlement decision.
decisions.recommendation: Rank approved service categories, cite the phrases that drove the match, and ask a focused question when confidence is low.

data.summary: Permission-cleared request text paired with final service categories, clarification turns, language, channel, and routing outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: reviewed routing history exists; historical misroutes must not become labels
data.risk: Past routing may encode unequal access or staff shortcuts; rare needs and languages can disappear in aggregate metrics.

method.output: Ranked service categories, confidence, and a clarification question when needed
method.technique: Multilingual text classification with calibrated abstention and approved service taxonomy

metric.technical: Macro precision and recall, calibration, abstention quality, and performance by language and service category.
metric.business: Improve first-route accuracy from the 14% misroute baseline and reduce repeat explanations without suppressing escalation.
metric.baseline: 12,000 monthly requests; 19% need clarification and 14% are initially misrouted

human.checkpoint: Review uncertain or urgent requests, correct the category, and preserve the resident's original wording.
human.falsePositiveCost: A plausible but wrong category sends the resident through another avoidable transfer.
human.falseNegativeCost: The system fails to surface a relevant service or urgent need.

decisions.label: Which authority has jurisdiction?
decisions.wrongCost: A request sits with an office that cannot act
decisions.testAnswer: No. Service area, address, program ownership, and inter-agency agreements are published constraints.
decisions.why: Jurisdiction should be explicit, versioned, and explainable rather than inferred from historical transfers.
decisions.recommendation: Resolve jurisdiction through the governed service catalog and route unknown boundaries for catalog maintenance.

decisions.label: Does the request meet the stated service criteria?
decisions.wrongCost: An eligible resident is blocked, or an ineligible case consumes scarce capacity
decisions.testAnswer: No. Stated eligibility conditions and required evidence belong in policy logic, not a model trained on past approvals.
decisions.why: Rules preserve transparency, appealability, and the distinction between missing evidence and ineligibility.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate only approved criteria, show the reason and policy source, and never infer protected or missing facts.

decisions.label: Should this request update an existing open case?
decisions.wrongCost: Duplicate work is created, or unrelated residents are merged
decisions.testAnswer: No for exact identifiers and case references. Ambiguous identity matches must be reviewed rather than guessed.
decisions.why: Controlled duplicate handling is workflow execution once identity and open-case keys are established.
decisions.recommendation: Merge only on approved exact keys; present ambiguous candidates to staff without automatic consolidation.

decisions.label: Which office or provider should receive the case?
decisions.wrongCost: A resident waits while another provider has suitable capacity
decisions.testAnswer: The choice balances capacity, location, accessibility, specialization, language, and appointment constraints.
decisions.why: The assignment objective and constraints can be stated and audited directly.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize among eligible providers and expose the constraint that drove each assignment or failure to assign.

decisions.label: How should the next step be explained to the resident?
decisions.frequency: Every routed, clarified, or ineligible request
decisions.wrongCost: The resident misunderstands the next step, misses evidence, or receives an unsupported promise
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can turn grounded service facts and rule outcomes into accessible language, but staff must verify consequential guidance.
decisions.why: The output is a communication artifact inside the workflow, not the eligibility or exception decision.
decisions.recommendation: Draft a plain-language explanation from the request, cited catalog entry, rule result, and approved accessibility guidance.

data.summary: Original request, approved service descriptions, rule outcomes, required evidence, accessibility guidance, and supported languages.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: approved service content is versioned; translations require review
data.risk: A fluent message can invent eligibility, deadlines, availability, or commitments that no source supports.

method.output: Grounded next-step explanation or focused request for missing information
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation constrained to service facts and deterministic rule results

metric.technical: Groundedness, unsupported-commitment rate, required-information coverage, and accessibility review pass rate.
metric.business: Reduce repeat contacts, clarification cycles, and abandoned requests while maintaining equitable comprehension.
metric.baseline: 19% of requests currently need at least one clarification cycle

human.checkpoint: Verify service facts, rule result, tone, language, accessibility, and any requested evidence before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The message promises service, eligibility, or timing that is not supported.
human.falseNegativeCost: The message omits a required next step and forces another contact.

decisions.label: Does this request need an exception or safeguarding response?
decisions.wrongCost: A vulnerable resident is missed, or a routine case is escalated intrusively
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own discretionary exception or safeguarding action. Context, consent, policy, and accountable judgment matter.
decisions.why: AI may surface evidence, but a trained caseworker must interpret urgency and authorize exceptional handling.
decisions.recommendation: Provide the original request, source facts, rule outcomes, and escalation guidance to an accountable caseworker.

title: One Day of Fleet Dispatch
subtitle: From promised jobs to safe routes under disruption
learningObjective: Separate travel prediction, route optimization, deterministic safety checks, controlled automation, customer communication, and dispatcher authority.
throughline: Prediction estimates what may happen; optimization chooses under constraints; the dispatcher owns the risky override.

introduction.title: Why a fleet plan keeps changing after dispatch
introduction.context: Daily fleet dispatch converts customer commitments into executable vehicle routes while balancing vehicle capacity, promised delivery windows, legal driver-hour limits, vehicle condition, traffic, and weather. Even a workable morning plan can become invalid when demand exceeds capacity, a vehicle breaks down, roads change, or a delivery promise becomes unlikely to hold.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows a day of jobs from input validation through lateness prediction, route optimization, plan approval, and execution. During disruptions it checks non-negotiable safety and legal limits, recalculates recovery options, requires a dispatcher to approve changes to service promises, and prepares evidence-based customer updates.
introduction.startsWhen: Dispatch receives the day's jobs, customer promises, available vehicles, drivers, and operating conditions.
introduction.endsWhen: Jobs are completed safely and any disruption, changed promise, or authorized tradeoff is communicated and recorded.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Jobs, fleet state, traffic, weather, promises

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Validate, predict, optimize, dispatch

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Late risk? Best route? Replan? Override?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Release, drive, reassign, or notify

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Safe completion with visible service tradeoffs

decisions.label: Are jobs, locations, vehicles, and constraints valid?
decisions.wrongCost: The solver returns a route that cannot be executed
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required fields, coordinate quality, vehicle status, hours limits, and service windows are explicit checks.
decisions.why: Optimization and prediction should never receive inputs that already violate known constraints.
decisions.recommendation: Fail closed on invalid or stale inputs and show the exact field or constraint that needs repair.

decisions.label: Which jobs are likely to miss their service window?
decisions.wrongCost: A preventable late promise, or costly buffer added to every route
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. New outcomes reveal changing travel times across traffic, weather, location, season, stop sequence, and vehicle conditions.
decisions.why: The output is a calibrated probability and expected amount of future lateness over a defined route horizon.
decisions.recommendation: Predict travel time and late risk with uncertainty; pass those estimates into the route solver rather than asking the model to choose routes.

data.summary: Planned and actual arrival events joined to routes, stops, traffic, weather, vehicle, driver-hours, and service-window context.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: event timestamps exist; reason codes for dwell and failed stops need cleanup
data.risk: Completed routes exclude cancelled and failed jobs unless outcomes are joined carefully; location and shift coverage can be uneven.

method.output: Expected arrival and probability of missing each service window
method.technique: Calibrated travel-time prediction with route-context and disruption features

metric.technical: Arrival-time MAE, late-event recall, calibration, and performance on the worst 5% of misses.
metric.business: Reduce the 8.5% late-job baseline and avoidable replanning without inflating route cost or unsafe pressure on drivers.
metric.baseline: 420 daily jobs with 8.5% late and 14 disruptions requiring attention

human.checkpoint: Review drift, extreme misses, route segments, and operational changes before estimates affect service promises.
human.falsePositiveCost: An overly pessimistic estimate creates unnecessary buffer, cost, or customer concern.
human.falseNegativeCost: A confident late miss breaks a promise and leaves the dispatcher no recovery time.

decisions.label: What is the best feasible route plan?
decisions.wrongCost: Excess distance, missed windows, unserved jobs, or infeasible driver work
decisions.testAnswer: No historical imitation is required when the objective and constraints can be written explicitly.
decisions.why: This is a vehicle-routing allocation problem using predicted travel time as one input.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize cost and service subject to capacity, hours, skills, windows, safety, and vehicle constraints; expose infeasibility.

decisions.label: Can this approved route plan be released?
decisions.wrongCost: Drivers receive conflicting or unauthorized work
decisions.testAnswer: No. Release follows explicit validation, plan version, authorization, and driver acknowledgment rules.
decisions.why: This is audited execution after decisions are complete, not another model judgment.
decisions.recommendation: Publish only the latest approved feasible plan, record acknowledgments, and prevent stale-plan dispatch.

decisions.label: Can the current route continue safely?
decisions.wrongCost: An unsafe or legally invalid route continues, or a minor event triggers needless replanning
decisions.testAnswer: No for vehicle safety, driver hours, road closure, and mandatory service constraints.
decisions.why: Known legal and safety boundaries must be deterministic and fail closed.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate hard constraints first; continue only when they pass and send the changed state to replanning otherwise.

decisions.label: What is the best feasible recovery plan?
decisions.wrongCost: The fleet recovers slowly, violates a constraint, or sacrifices the wrong commitments
decisions.testAnswer: The new state changes constraints and objective tradeoffs; the solver should recompute rather than a model inventing an action.
decisions.why: Recovery is the same constrained allocation problem with updated vehicles, jobs, times, and promises.
decisions.recommendation: Re-solve from the current state, preserve hard constraints, and present tradeoff options when no plan meets every promise.

decisions.label: What should the affected customer be told?
decisions.frequency: Every disruption that changes a promise
decisions.wrongCost: A false ETA or unsupported remedy damages trust and creates repeat contact
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can turn grounded route facts and approved policy into a clear update, but it must not invent an ETA or remedy.
decisions.why: The output is a communication artifact grounded in the approved recovery plan.
decisions.recommendation: Draft from the latest plan version, event evidence, revised ETA, service policy, and approved remedy options; require review before sending.

data.summary: Latest approved route, observed disruption, revised ETA, customer promise, communication history, and service policy.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: route versions are controlled and approved communication policy is retrievable
data.risk: Stale route state can produce a polished but incorrect ETA or compensation promise.

method.output: Grounded disruption update with revised expectation and approved next step
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation constrained to the current route plan and service policy

metric.technical: Groundedness, stale-plan use, unsupported-promise rate, and required-fact coverage.
metric.business: Improve reviewer acceptance and reduce repeat contacts without increasing compensation errors or customer complaints.
metric.baseline: 14 daily disruptions create manual replanning and communication work

human.checkpoint: Verify the current plan version, ETA, customer impact, policy, and remedy before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The customer receives an unsupported promise, unnecessary remedy, or wrong ETA.
human.falseNegativeCost: A material delay or required next step is omitted and the customer cannot respond.

decisions.label: Should a service tradeoff or operational override be authorized?
decisions.frequency: Only when no plan satisfies every service goal
decisions.wrongCost: Safety or legal limits are breached, or a recoverable service promise is abandoned
decisions.testAnswer: Hard safety constraints are never overridable; accountable staff must own any permitted service tradeoff among feasible options.
decisions.why: The solver can expose options and consequences, but it does not carry authority for consequential operational choices.
decisions.recommendation: Block hard-constraint violations and require dispatcher rationale for any permitted customer or cost tradeoff.

title: One Referral to an Accepted Appointment
subtitle: From submitted evidence to coordinated specialty access
learningObjective: Separate document interpretation, specialty classification, policy rules, capacity optimization, delay prediction, communication support, and accountable urgency escalation.
throughline: Use AI to prepare and prioritize administrative work; never let it diagnose, determine treatment, or own clinical urgency.

introduction.title: Why one referral crosses so many operational boundaries
introduction.context: A healthcare referral is the operational request that moves a patient from a referring provider toward another service or specialty. Before an appointment can be accepted, teams may need readable records, the correct service category, required evidence, authorization status, available capacity, and a reliable way to contact the patient. This scenario coordinates those administrative steps only; it does not diagnose, recommend treatment, or perform clinical triage.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one synthetic referral from document intake through evidence extraction, specialty routing, human urgency review, deterministic requirement and authorization checks, appointment optimization, delay-risk prediction, grounded communication, and final acceptance. Exception paths cover unreadable or missing records, unmet service requirements, uncertain routing, pending authorization, limited capacity, and patient non-response.
introduction.startsWhen: A referring provider submits a referral packet and requested service for a patient.
introduction.endsWhen: The receiving team accepts a scheduled appointment, or a qualified human accepts an urgent escalation with an auditable handoff.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Referral, records, requested service, patient contact

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Extract, route, verify, authorize, coordinate

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Complete? Which service? Authorized? At risk?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Clarify, escalate, schedule, or communicate

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Accepted appointment or qualified urgent handoff

decisions.label: Can the referral evidence be interpreted reliably?
decisions.wrongCost: Incorrect facts contaminate routing and authorization, or a usable referral is delayed
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Document type, layout, image quality, and reviewed field corrections improve interpretation across variable referral records.
decisions.why: The system must classify document evidence, extract operational fields, cite their source, and abstain when confidence is low.
decisions.recommendation: Extract referral facts with field-level citations and confidence; route low-confidence or missing evidence to human review.

data.summary: Synthetic referral forms and attached records paired with reviewed document classes, field values, source regions, and correction outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic assumption: representative packet layouts and reviewed corrections are available
data.risk: Historical reviewer corrections can be inconsistent, and aggregate accuracy can hide weak performance on rare record types.

method.output: Document class, operational fields, source citations, and confidence
method.technique: Layout-aware document classification and extraction with field-level abstention

metric.technical: Document macro F1, field precision and recall, citation accuracy, and low-confidence coverage by record type.
metric.business: Reduce first-pass preparation and repeated evidence requests without increasing incorrectly completed referrals.
metric.baseline: 28% of 6,000 synthetic monthly referrals need evidence clarification

human.checkpoint: Verify uncertain values against the source record and request missing evidence without interpreting clinical meaning.
human.falsePositiveCost: An incorrect extracted fact is treated as reliable and affects later administrative checks.
human.falseNegativeCost: Readable evidence is rejected and the patient or referring team repeats work.

decisions.label: Which specialty or service should receive the referral?
decisions.wrongCost: The referral reaches the wrong service, is transferred repeatedly, or waits in the wrong queue
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Reviewed routing outcomes reveal varied referring language and overlapping service descriptions that improve ranked service matching.
decisions.why: The output is an administrative service category with confidence, not a diagnosis, treatment recommendation, or clinical priority.
decisions.recommendation: Rank approved service categories, show the evidence behind the match, and require coordinator confirmation for low confidence.

data.summary: Synthetic referral descriptions, requested services, approved service taxonomy, final confirmed destinations, and transfer outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic assumption: service taxonomy is versioned and confirmed routing outcomes are retained
data.risk: Past routing shortcuts can become labels, and rare services can disappear inside aggregate accuracy.

method.output: Ranked service categories with confidence and cited referral evidence
method.technique: Calibrated text and structured-feature classification over an approved service taxonomy

metric.technical: Macro precision and recall, top-two recall, calibration, and abstention quality by service category.
metric.business: Improve first-route accuracy and reduce avoidable transfers while preserving coordinator review for ambiguity.
metric.baseline: Synthetic baseline to be established from manually reviewed referral routes

human.checkpoint: Confirm uncertain service matches and every route that could alter clinical review responsibility.
human.falsePositiveCost: A plausible but wrong service accepts work it cannot complete.
human.falseNegativeCost: A relevant service is omitted and coordination is delayed.

decisions.label: Does this referral need qualified urgent review?
decisions.frequency: Every referral after initial service matching
decisions.wrongCost: An urgent concern follows routine scheduling, or a routine referral is escalated unnecessarily
decisions.testAnswer: No model in this scenario may determine clinical urgency. An approved rule may surface a stated flag, but a qualified human owns the interpretation and handoff.
decisions.why: Urgency can affect clinical responsibility and patient safety; administrative AI must not infer diagnosis or priority.
decisions.recommendation: Show the original referral evidence and approved escalation guidance to a qualified human; never generate an autonomous urgency score.

decisions.label: Are the explicit service requirements met?
decisions.wrongCost: An incomplete referral advances, or unnecessary evidence is requested
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required documents and operational prerequisites belong in versioned policy tables, not a model trained on historical acceptance.
decisions.why: Explicit requirements must remain transparent, appealable, and distinguish missing evidence from an unsupported request.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate versioned service requirements and return each missing item with its policy source.

decisions.label: Is required authorization present and current?
decisions.frequency: Every referral whose policy path requires authorization
decisions.wrongCost: A patient is scheduled without required approval, or an authorized referral waits unnecessarily
decisions.testAnswer: No. Authorization requirement, status, effective period, and required reference fields are explicit administrative facts.
decisions.why: The system should expose the source status and missing fields rather than infer authorization from historical scheduling behavior.
decisions.recommendation: Check approved authorization sources and fail closed to a human work queue when status is missing, expired, or inconsistent.

decisions.label: Which eligible location and appointment slot should be offered?
decisions.wrongCost: A patient receives an infeasible option while suitable capacity remains unused
decisions.testAnswer: The choice balances eligible service, capacity, location, accessibility, patient availability, and appointment constraints.
decisions.why: The objective and hard constraints can be stated and audited directly; a solver should not imitate historical scheduling inequities.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize among eligible slots, expose binding constraints, and return no solution when every option violates a hard requirement.

decisions.label: Is this referral likely to miss its coordination target?
decisions.frequency: At intake and after each unresolved handoff
decisions.wrongCost: A referral stalls without attention, or staff create unnecessary outreach for low-risk cases
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Mature outcomes can reveal changing combinations of missing evidence, authorization delay, capacity, prior outreach, and elapsed time.
decisions.why: The output is the probability of an administrative outcome over a defined time horizon, not a prediction of health or treatment need.
decisions.recommendation: Predict coordination delay with calibrated uncertainty and use it to prioritize staff attention, never clinical priority.

data.summary: Synthetic referral events joined to evidence status, authorization status, capacity, outreach attempts, and confirmed scheduling outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic assumption: event timestamps and final coordination outcomes are consistently captured
data.risk: Historical delays can reflect access inequities or service constraints rather than patient willingness.

method.output: Probability that the referral remains unscheduled beyond the administrative target window
method.technique: Calibrated supervised prediction over point-in-time referral event features

metric.technical: Calibration, late-case recall at outreach capacity, precision-recall AUC, and performance by service and access channel.
metric.business: Increase useful coordinator lead time and completed referrals without creating excessive outreach or unequal intervention burden.
metric.baseline: Synthetic target window and intervention capacity must be validated before implementation

human.checkpoint: Review operational causes and choose outreach or escalation; do not infer patient motivation or clinical urgency.
human.falsePositiveCost: Staff create unnecessary contact and burden for a referral already progressing normally.
human.falseNegativeCost: A preventable administrative delay remains invisible until the target window is missed.

decisions.label: How should the next administrative step be explained?
decisions.frequency: Every clarification, authorization update, or appointment offer
decisions.wrongCost: The patient or referring team receives an unsupported instruction, wrong status, or missing next step
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can turn verified referral facts and approved policy into accessible communication, but staff must review every status and action.
decisions.why: The output is an administrative message grounded in evidence; it must refuse diagnosis, treatment advice, and unsupported urgency language.
decisions.recommendation: Draft from verified status, missing items, available options, approved templates, and contact preferences; require coordinator approval before sending.

data.summary: Verified referral status, approved requirements, authorization facts, appointment options, communication history, and accessibility preferences.
data.owner: Referral operations, communications, and policy governance
data.readiness: Synthetic assumption: status sources and approved message templates are versioned
data.risk: A fluent message can invent status, promise availability, or drift into diagnosis or treatment guidance.

method.output: Grounded administrative message with cited status and a clear next action
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation constrained to verified referral facts and approved communication policy

metric.technical: Groundedness, unsupported-claim rate, required-action coverage, and prohibited clinical-content rate.
metric.business: Improve reviewer acceptance and reduce repeat contacts without increasing incorrect instructions or missed actions.
metric.baseline: Synthetic communication baseline to be established from reviewed referral messages

human.checkpoint: Verify status, requested evidence, appointment option, accessibility, and absence of clinical advice before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The message states an unsupported requirement, promise, or clinical implication.
human.falseNegativeCost: The message omits a necessary next step and creates another coordination loop.

title: One Pediatric Chest X-ray
subtitle: From imaging order to accountable clinical action
learningObjective: Map image acquisition and review, separate technical quality, learned classification, policy routing, radiologist interpretation, and clinician authority.
throughline: The model may change review order; it does not interpret the image, diagnose a patient, or choose treatment.

introduction.title: What happens between an imaging order and a clinical action?
introduction.context: A chest X-ray model is only one bounded component inside a larger care workflow. Before a score can influence review order, the request and image must be usable. After routing, a radiologist still interprets the study and a clinician combines that report with symptoms, history, examination, and other evidence.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one pediatric chest X-ray through order and identity checks, image acquisition, technical-quality review, CNN scoring, cutoff-based queue routing, radiologist interpretation, required-result communication, clinician decision-making, and outcome monitoring. Exception paths expose identity correction, image recapture, and priority routing.
introduction.startsWhen: A clinician places a chest X-ray order and the imaging service receives the request.
introduction.endsWhen: A radiologist report reaches the care team and a clinician owns the documented next action.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Order, identity, acquired image, limited context

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Verify, acquire, quality-check, score, interpret

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Usable image? Which queue? What finding and action?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Recapture, route, report, communicate, or treat

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Qualified interpretation and accountable clinical action

decisions.label: Do the patient, order, and examination identifiers match?
decisions.wrongCost: The wrong patient or examination could enter the workflow, or a valid request could be delayed
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required identifiers, order status, examination type, and matching rules are explicit safety controls.
decisions.why: Identity and order validation must be deterministic, auditable, and corrected at the source rather than inferred from pixels.
decisions.recommendation: Use required-field, identifier-match, order-status, and examination-protocol checks before acquisition and scoring.

decisions.label: Is the acquired image technically usable for the ordinary model path?
decisions.owner: Imaging technologist with technical quality controls
decisions.wrongCost: An unusable image receives a confident-looking score, or an acceptable image is recaptured unnecessarily
decisions.testAnswer: Simple exposure and focus bounds can be stated directly, while a technologist must resolve uncertainty and clinical acquisition issues.
decisions.why: The quality gate controls whether scoring may run. It does not classify disease and should not silently repair or reinterpret a failed image.
decisions.recommendation: Apply versioned technical checks, stop scoring when they fail, and route to recapture or qualified manual quality review.

decisions.label: How strongly does this image resemble pneumonia-labeled training examples?
decisions.frequency: Every technically usable image inside the intended input boundary
decisions.wrongCost: A pneumonia-labeled study remains later in the queue, or a normal-labeled study consumes scarce priority capacity
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. A CNN learns recurring spatial patterns from labeled images rather than applying one hand-written brightness or texture rule.
decisions.why: The model produces a ranking score associated with the benchmark label. It does not interpret the image, estimate patient risk, or output a diagnosis.
decisions.recommendation: Produce a bounded ranking score, then keep technical-quality checks, queue policy, interpretation, diagnosis, and treatment outside the model.

data.summary: Checksum-verified PneumoniaMNIST pediatric chest X-rays with source-defined train, validation, and held-out test splits.
data.owner: Benchmark publisher and classroom artifact steward
data.readiness: Prepared public benchmark for education; not representative evidence for clinical deployment
data.risk: The benchmark is narrow, downsampled, and lacks symptoms, history, site diversity, acquisition metadata, localization labels, and prospective outcomes.

method.output: An uncalibrated ranking score used only for priority or standard review routing
method.technique: Compact four-block PyTorch CNN with a validation-selected operating cutoff

metric.technical: On 624 held-out benchmark images: 93.3% sensitivity and 85.9% specificity at the validation-selected 0.748 cutoff.
metric.business: Before any real use, measure time to qualified interpretation, priority workload, recapture burden, and subgroup or site performance.
metric.baseline: The teaching replay routes 397 of 624 held-out studies to priority review; this is not a clinical operating target.

human.role: Radiologist, followed by the treating clinician
human.checkpoint: Interpret every study independently of the model score and combine the report with the complete patient context before clinical action.
human.falsePositiveCost: A normal-labeled study consumes priority capacity and may delay other work.
human.falseNegativeCost: A pneumonia-labeled study remains in standard review and may wait longer for interpretation.

decisions.label: Is the model score at or above the approved review cutoff?
decisions.frequency: Every image that receives a model score
decisions.wrongCost: The priority queue exceeds capacity, or more pneumonia-labeled studies remain in standard review
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the score and approved cutoff are available, the branch is a deterministic comparison rather than another learned prediction.
decisions.why: Keeping the cutoff outside the model makes the sensitivity and workload tradeoff visible, versioned, and change-controlled.
decisions.recommendation: Select the cutoff on validation data, freeze it before test evaluation, record the policy version, and monitor both queues.

decisions.label: What does the chest X-ray show?
decisions.frequency: Every study in priority and standard review
decisions.wrongCost: A finding is missed, overstated, or interpreted without necessary context
decisions.testAnswer: The model score is not an image interpretation. A radiologist evaluates image findings, limitations, comparisons, and available context.
decisions.why: PneumoniaMNIST supplies whole-image labels, not validated lesion locations, clinical reasoning, diagnoses, or treatment decisions.
decisions.recommendation: Require qualified interpretation for every image and allow the radiologist to ignore, challenge, and report limitations of model output.

decisions.label: Does the interpreted finding require an urgent qualified handoff?
decisions.wrongCost: A time-sensitive finding is not communicated promptly, or routine work creates unnecessary escalation
decisions.testAnswer: Communication requirements may include explicit policy, but a qualified professional must connect the interpreted finding to the required handoff.
decisions.why: The model's queue route cannot determine clinical urgency or replace closed-loop communication of an interpreted result.
decisions.recommendation: Use approved escalation rules and documented receipt while keeping urgency interpretation and handoff ownership with qualified staff.

decisions.label: What clinical action, if any, should follow the radiologist report?
decisions.frequency: Every report returned to the care team
decisions.wrongCost: Care is delayed, unnecessary, or based on an image without the rest of the patient context
decisions.testAnswer: The decision combines the report with symptoms, history, examination, tests, patient preferences, and treatment guidance unavailable to the model.
decisions.why: Neither the CNN score nor the radiograph alone defines a diagnosis or treatment plan.
decisions.recommendation: Present the signed report and relevant context to the treating clinician; never convert the queue route into diagnosis or treatment.

title: One Monthly Risk Review
subtitle: From account snapshot to an explainable intervention
learningObjective: Map a monthly credit-risk review as an operating process, price the review decision with a cost rule, and keep intervention and explanation in human hands.
throughline: The model ranks accounts; a cost rule sizes the queue; people decide what happens to a customer.

introduction.title: What happens in a card issuer's monthly credit-risk review?
introduction.context: A card issuer watches its existing customers, not just new applicants. Every month it asks one question about each account: is this customer about to miss a payment? Catching trouble early lets the bank offer help — a call, a payment plan — before a missed payment becomes a loss. But the review team can look at only a few hundred of 30,000 accounts, and any step that hurts a customer must, by law, come with specific written reasons the customer can understand.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one monthly cycle: a snapshot of each account's recent behavior is assembled and checked for unusable data, a model estimates the chance of a missed payment, a cost rule decides which accounts are worth one of the team's limited reviews, an analyst chooses the intervention, compliance owns any notice that must explain itself, and next month's real outcome is logged to keep score on the model. Exception paths reveal the excluded-account log and the vague-reasons loop.
introduction.startsWhen: The monthly account snapshot — six months of bills, payments, and repayment status for every account — is assembled.
introduction.endsWhen: The intervention decision is recorded for every flagged account and the next month's actual payment outcome is logged.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Credit limit and six months of bills, payments, repayment status

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Assemble snapshot, check validity, score, rank the queue

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Data usable? Miss likely? Worth a review? Which intervention?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Offer help, adjust the account, send a notice, or do nothing

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Next month's payment made or missed, logged against the call

baseline.label: miss the next payment
baseline.note: Historical rate in the classroom dataset

baseline.label: accounts the team can review monthly
baseline.note: Classroom staffing assumption, sized to the review policy

baseline.label: fully loaded cost of one review and outreach
baseline.note: Classroom cost assumption used by the review policy

baseline.label: average balance at risk per account
baseline.note: Average unpaid balance capped at the credit limit, measured in the classroom dataset

nodes.label: Offer outreach or a payment plan
Is the model still on target?

decisions.label: Are the account's fields present and its codes known?
decisions.wrongCost: A garbled account gets a meaningless score, or a scoreable account is silently dropped
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required fields and the list of known codes are fixed requirements; more history does not change them.
decisions.why: The source data carries real quirks — undocumented category codes — and the safe response is an explicit, auditable check, not a guess.
decisions.recommendation: Check field presence and known codes deterministically; exclude and log failures instead of scoring them.

decisions.label: How likely is this account to miss its next payment?
decisions.frequency: Every valid account, once a month
decisions.wrongCost: A scarce review is wasted on a fine account, or a preventable miss goes unreviewed
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Each month's real outcomes show which behavior patterns preceded a missed payment, and those patterns shift with the economy.
decisions.why: No fixed rule captures how repayment status, bills, and payments combine across six months; the relationship is learned from thousands of past outcomes.
decisions.recommendation: Estimate a probability with visible reason codes, and let the cost policy and the analyst — not the score — decide what happens.

data.summary: One row per account: credit limit plus six months of monthly repayment status, bill amounts, and payment amounts, joined to whether the next payment was missed. Sex, marriage, and age exist in the source data but are deliberately excluded because fair-lending law restricts their use in credit decisions.
data.readiness: Prepared classroom dataset: 30,000 real anonymized accounts from one issuer, complete fields, converted once at build time
data.risk: The accounts come from one issuer in one era, and behavior fields can still stand in for the excluded demographics — exclusion is necessary, not sufficient.

method.output: Probability of a missed payment next month
method.technique: Interpretable logistic regression compared against gradient boosting on the same split, with per-account reason codes

metric.technical: AUC on held-out accounts, reported with and without the excluded demographic fields so the fairness cost is measured, not asserted.
metric.business: Net review savings: the value of misses prevented by early help, minus the cost of every analyst review the policy triggers.
metric.baseline: Rank accounts by months currently behind and review up to the 600-account monthly capacity

human.checkpoint: Reviews each flagged account and chooses the intervention; the score never changes an account by itself.
human.falsePositiveCost: An analyst spends one of 600 monthly reviews, at NT$1,000, on an account that was never in trouble.
human.falseNegativeCost: A preventable missed payment becomes a real loss on an average NT$140,000 balance at risk.

decisions.label: Is this account worth one of the team's limited reviews?
decisions.wrongCost: The queue outgrows the 600-review capacity, or costly accounts skip review
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the probability, the balance at risk, and the review cost are set, the comparison is arithmetic.
decisions.why: The model estimates risk; the business sets the prices. Review when the expected loss avoided exceeds the review cost — a rule anyone can audit and re-tune.
decisions.recommendation: Version the cost parameters, publish the implied queue size, and keep a fixed-capacity fallback if the queue outgrows the team.

decisions.label: What should happen to this account, if anything?
decisions.frequency: Every account in the monthly review queue
decisions.wrongCost: A struggling customer gets no help, or a fine customer is treated as a risk and loses trust
decisions.testAnswer: The score is a probability, not a verdict. Choosing between outreach, a payment plan, a limit review, or nothing takes context the model never sees.
decisions.why: This is the decision that touches the customer. The model never contacts anyone, never changes a limit, and never labels anyone a defaulter.
decisions.recommendation: Show the analyst the score, the reason codes, and the account history; record every choice, including no action.

decisions.label: Can we give this customer specific reasons for an adverse step?
decisions.wrongCost: A legally required notice goes out vague or wrong, or a defensible step is delayed
decisions.verdictLabel: Keep the human — compliance owns it
decisions.testAnswer: More data does not change the duty. The law requires specific principal reasons a customer can act on; a score alone is explicitly not enough.
decisions.why: If the model cannot support plain-language reasons for this account, the bank may not take the model-driven step — explainability is a legal requirement, not a preference.
decisions.recommendation: Turn the top reason codes into plain sentences, have compliance approve the notice, and send the case back if the reasons are too vague.

decisions.label: Is the model still ranking accounts the way outcomes say it should?
decisions.wrongCost: A drifting model quietly mis-ranks accounts for months before anyone notices
decisions.testAnswer: No for the check itself: comparing predicted and actual miss rates against agreed limits is bookkeeping. What it triggers — retraining — uses new data.
decisions.why: Every logged outcome is a free test of last month's predictions; a standing comparison catches drift without waiting for a crisis.
decisions.recommendation: Track predicted-versus-actual rates and queue results on a dashboard, and open a retraining review when they cross an agreed line.

title: One Customer Complaint
subtitle: From intake to the right team before the clock runs out
learningObjective: Map a complaint desk that answers on a deadline, decide where reading text with a model helps, and keep judgment about the complaint itself with people.
throughline: The model reads the words and names a team; people judge the complaint and write the answer.

introduction.title: What happens after a customer complains to a bank?
introduction.context: When someone complains to a bank about a financial product — through the website, by mail, or forwarded by a government regulator — the bank is expected to send a substantive answer within about 15 days. The complaint arrives as ordinary written English, but the bank is organized into specialist teams by product. Sending a mortgage complaint to the credit-card team wastes days the clock does not give back, so the first and most repeated decision is simply: who should read this?
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one complaint through logging and a completeness check, a model that reads the narrative and names a likely team, a confidence gate that chooses between automatic routing and the human triage desk, the specialist team's investigation and drafted answer, an approval step, and a monthly check on how often the routing was right. Exception paths reveal the missing-details loop and the bounce-back that corrects a misrouted case.
introduction.startsWhen: A complaint arrives through the web form, by mail, or as a regulator forwarding, and is logged with a response due date.
introduction.endsWhen: An approved response is sent within the response window and the final team and routing outcome are logged.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: The complaint text, product hints, channel, and the due date

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Log, check completeness, classify, route, investigate

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Complete? Which team? Confident enough to auto-route?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Auto-route, hand to triage, bounce back, send the answer

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: An approved response on time, and a routing record to learn from

baseline.label: lost when a complaint is misrouted

decisions.label: Does the complaint carry enough detail to route?
decisions.wrongCost: A vague complaint bounces between teams, or a customer is asked for details the bank already holds
decisions.testAnswer: No. The required pieces — a product hint, an account link, a narrative or document — are a checklist known in advance.
decisions.why: Completeness is a fixed requirement, and the clock is already running while it is checked; the check must be instant and consistent.
decisions.recommendation: Check required fields deterministically and ask the customer for exactly what is missing, nothing more.

decisions.label: Which specialist team should take this complaint?
decisions.wrongCost: Days of a 15-day response clock lost in the wrong queue
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Customers keep finding new ways to describe the same problems, and every resolved case shows which team each wording really belonged to.
decisions.why: No rulebook can list every way someone describes a mortgage problem or a stolen card; the mapping from words to teams is learned from thousands of resolved complaints.
decisions.recommendation: Predict a team with a confidence score, show the weighted words behind the call, and auto-route only above the threshold.

data.summary: Historical complaints pairing the narrative a customer wrote with the product team that finally resolved it, drawn from the public CFPB complaint database. Narratives appear only when the consumer opted in, and personal details are already masked at the source.
data.owner: Complaint operations and the quality team
data.readiness: Public US-government data; a filtered classroom sample with consolidated team labels, committed once at build time
fields: Product team label from past resolutions
data.risk: Product labels were renamed over the years and one team dominates recent volume, so labels need consolidation and the model can lean toward the biggest class.

method.output: A team label with a confidence score
method.technique: TF-IDF word counts with logistic regression, so the weighted words are the visible reasons for each route

metric.technical: Accuracy averaged evenly across teams, plus coverage — the share of complaints routed automatically at the chosen confidence threshold.
