metric.business: Days saved on the response clock by cutting misroutes and their three-day delay, compared with hand-triaging everything.
metric.baseline: All 9,000 monthly complaints read and assigned by the six-person triage desk

human.checkpoint: Any agent can re-route a complaint that landed wrong; the triage desk reads everything below the confidence threshold.
human.falsePositiveCost: A confident but wrong route sends the complaint to the wrong specialists and burns clock days before anyone notices.
human.falseNegativeCost: An over-cautious model routes routine complaints to triage and buries the small desk in work it did not need.

decisions.label: Is the model confident enough to route without a person?
decisions.wrongCost: Confident mistakes route themselves, or the triage desk drowns in routine mail
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the confidence score and the approved threshold exist, the branch is a comparison — though the threshold is re-chosen from measured results.
decisions.why: The model reports confidence; the business decides how much confidence buys an automatic route. Keeping the threshold outside the model makes the tradeoff visible and tunable.
decisions.recommendation: Version the threshold, log which policy routed each complaint, and watch triage volume against its six-person staffing.

decisions.label: How should the complaint be resolved?
decisions.wrongCost: A real problem is dismissed, or the bank concedes something it never owed
decisions.testAnswer: Whether the customer is right takes account records, policy, and accountable judgment — not a pattern score over words.
decisions.why: The model only names a team. It never judges the complaint's merit, never drafts the answer, and never contacts the consumer.
decisions.recommendation: Keep resolution with the specialist, and make bouncing a misrouted case back to triage one click, so every misroute is corrected and logged.

decisions.label: Is the response ready to send?
decisions.wrongCost: A wrong or unclear answer goes to the customer — and onto a regulated record — under deadline pressure
decisions.testAnswer: No. This is accountability, not pattern-finding: a named person must stand behind the answer the customer receives.
decisions.why: The response is the bank's official word on a regulated record, and deadline pressure is exactly when an approval step earns its keep.
decisions.recommendation: Require a named approver with the draft, the case file, and the remaining clock in one view before anything goes out.

decisions.label: Is the routing still landing complaints on the right teams?
decisions.frequency: Monthly, over a sample of closed cases
decisions.wrongCost: Routing quietly degrades as products and wording change, burning clock days at scale
decisions.testAnswer: No for the check: comparing the final team on each closed case with the first route is bookkeeping. What it triggers — retraining — uses new data.
decisions.why: Every re-routed case is a free label saying where the complaint really belonged; a standing monthly comparison turns those corrections into an accuracy report.
decisions.recommendation: Track re-route rates by team every month and open a model review when any team crosses an agreed line.

title: One Week of Depot Maintenance
subtitle: From the sensor stream to a closed work order
learningObjective: Map a maintenance depot's weekly planning as an operating process, price the alert threshold against callout and downtime costs, and keep the diagnosis and the safety call with a technician.
throughline: The model flags a fault that is developing now, within hours — it never forecasts days ahead; a threshold sizes the work list, and a technician decides what is actually wrong.

introduction.title: What happens in a transit depot's weekly maintenance planning?
introduction.context: A depot is the garage where a transit system's trains are serviced. Each train carries an air compressor — a pump that makes the compressed air the brakes and doors need. If that compressor fails while the train is in service, the train stops and passengers are stranded. Sensors on the unit report temperature and pressure every few seconds, so the depot is never short of data. What it is short of is technicians: a small crew can only pull a few units off the line each week, so somebody has to choose which ones.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one weekly planning cycle: the week's sensor readings are assembled and checked for gaps, six plain-language measures are built for every hour, a model scores how unusual each hour looks, a threshold decides which units get a work order and which only go on a watch list, a technician inspects and repairs, a safety check clears the unit back into service, and what was actually found is recorded against the alert. Exception paths reveal the sensor-gap log and the monthly recalibration loop.
introduction.startsWhen: The week's sensor stream from every monitored compressor is assembled and checked for gaps.
introduction.endsWhen: The work order is closed and what the technician actually found is recorded against the alert that raised it.

stages.description: A week of compressor readings: pressure, temperature, and motor activity

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Check for gaps, build six hourly measures, score each hour, rank the units

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Data fresh? Hour unusual? Worth a callout? What is actually wrong?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Raise a work order, watch the unit, repair it, or leave it running

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: What the technician found, logged against the alert that sent them

decisions.label: Are this unit's readings recent and complete enough to score?
decisions.frequency: Every unit, every hour of the weekly run
decisions.wrongCost: A stale or half-missing hour produces a confident-looking score built on nothing
decisions.testAnswer: No. How recent a reading must be, and how many minutes may be missing, are fixed requirements written down in advance.
decisions.why: About 7 percent of the classroom record is simply missing, and the gaps cluster in exactly the hours before a failure. Guessing through a gap is worse than admitting it.
decisions.recommendation: Check the timestamp and the count of readings deterministically; when an hour fails the check, produce no score at all and log the gap so the reliability review can see it.

decisions.label: How unusual does this hour look compared with the machine's normal behavior?
decisions.wrongCost: A technician is sent to a healthy machine, or a developing fault runs untreated toward a service interruption
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. What counts as normal is learned from months of the machine's own readings, and it is not something anyone can write down as a fixed limit per sensor.
decisions.why: No single sensor limit catches a developing air leak. The signal is how six measures move together, relative to what this machine usually does — and that is learned from its history, not declared.
decisions.recommendation: Publish an anomaly score with the measures that drove it, and let the threshold policy and the technician — never the score — decide what happens to the machine. Be explicit about what it claims: it detects a fault that is developing now, within hours; it does not forecast a failure days ahead, and it never locks out equipment.

data.summary: Real sensor readings from a transit compressor, averaged from roughly every ten seconds up to one-minute rows and then into six measures for each hour. The ground truth is four documented air-leak failures across seven months — only four — so results are read as examples, never as statistics.
data.readiness: Prepared classroom dataset: a real public air-production-unit record covering February to September, averaged and committed once at build time
fields: How much of the hour the compressor worked hard
How many times the compressor started during the hour
How many minutes it rested between bursts of work
How far pressure swings on each cycle
How fast pressure falls while the machine rests
data.risk: Only four documented failures exist, so nothing here supports a confident accuracy figure. Two of the six measures are undefined precisely when the machine never rests — during the worst failures — and quietly dropping those rows hides exactly the hours that matter.

method.output: An anomaly score, not a failure prediction
method.technique: For each measure, a one-sided distance from the machine's own typical value using a median center and a spread that ignores outliers, averaged across the six; compared against isolation forest and reconstruction methods, both of which raised far more false callouts at the same detection

metric.technical: Detection: were the documented failures scored above the line while they were happening, and how often did a clean hour raise a false callout — reported as a false-callout rate per month, not as an accuracy percentage.
metric.business: Net cost per month against two honest comparisons: never alerting at all, and inspecting every unit on a fixed schedule.
metric.baseline: Never alert and repair after the breakdown, or send a technician around every unit on a fixed inspection round

human.checkpoint: The technician goes to the unit, inspects it, and decides what is wrong and what to do; the score raises a work order and nothing more — it never locks out equipment and never certifies a machine as safe.
human.falsePositiveCost: A wasted callout: roughly $400 of technician time spent on a machine that turns out to be fine (classroom assumption).
human.falseNegativeCost: An unplanned service interruption: roughly $1,200 for every hour the fault runs, and about $22,000 once the unit has been out of service for 12 hours (classroom assumptions).

architecture: Outcome log and monthly recalibration review

decisions.label: Is this score high enough to spend a callout on?
decisions.wrongCost: Set low, technicians stop trusting the alerts; set high, a unit fails in service
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the score exists and the business has priced a callout against downtime, the branch is a comparison anyone can check by hand.
decisions.why: The model says how unusual the hour is; the business decides how unusual is worth $400. Keeping that line outside the model is what makes the trade-off visible, arguable, and adjustable.
decisions.recommendation: Version the threshold, route scores into work order, watch list, or no action, and publish how many callouts a month each setting implies before anyone changes it.

decisions.label: What is actually wrong with this machine, and what should be done about it?
decisions.wrongCost: A real fault is missed on a live inspection, or a healthy unit is stripped down for nothing
decisions.testAnswer: The score says an hour looked unusual. It cannot hear the machine, smell a hot bearing, or know that this unit was worked hard yesterday for reasons nobody logged.
decisions.why: In the classroom data a perfectly healthy compressor on a busy day scores 12.07 and the year's worst failure scores 12.08. No threshold separates them — only a person standing in front of the machine.
decisions.recommendation: Show the technician the score, the six measures that drove it, and the unit's recent history; record the finding either way, including "nothing found," because that is the label the system learns from.

decisions.label: Is this unit safe to put back into service?
decisions.wrongCost: A unit goes back into passenger service with the fault still on it
decisions.verdictLabel: Keep the human — safety owns it
decisions.testAnswer: More data does not change who is accountable. Somebody qualified has to sign that this machine is safe, and no score can carry that signature.
decisions.why: This is the module's safety boundary. The monitoring system may raise work, but it never takes equipment out of service and it never puts equipment back in.
decisions.recommendation: Require a named supervisor to clear the unit against the site's return-to-service checklist, and send it back to the bench if anything is unresolved.

decisions.label: Has the finding been recorded against the alert that raised it?
decisions.frequency: Every work order before it closes
decisions.wrongCost: The one thing that tells you whether the alert was right is never written down
decisions.testAnswer: No. The required pieces — what was found, what was replaced, hours spent, and whether the alert was justified — are a fixed checklist.
decisions.why: Four documented failures is all the ground truth this system starts with. Every closed work order is a new one, but only if somebody writes it down and it is tied back to the alert.
decisions.recommendation: Block closure until the finding is linked to the alert, and treat "nothing found" as a first-class result rather than a blank field.

decisions.label: Is the alert line still right for how hard the fleet is working now?
decisions.frequency: Monthly, with the previous month's outcomes in hand
decisions.wrongCost: A threshold tuned in spring floods the queue by summer, and technicians start ignoring the system
decisions.testAnswer: Machines get busier for reasons that have nothing to do with breaking — a new timetable, a hot month, a route change. Only someone who knows why the fleet's workload changed can say whether the line should move.
decisions.why: In the classroom data the same unchanged rule fires on 19 percent of clean April hours and 87 percent of clean August hours. An automatic rolling baseline fixes the flood but quietly absorbs slow-developing faults, so the trade-off has to be made by people who can see both costs.
decisions.recommendation: Review last month's alerts, callouts, and findings together each month; change the threshold deliberately and record why, rather than letting a rolling window move it silently.

title: One Technician's Question
subtitle: From a question at the machine to a verified, cited procedure
learningObjective: Map a procedure lookup as an operating process, treat a refusal as a designed outcome rather than a failure, and keep the authority to start work with the qualified person.
throughline: The assistant finds the passage and drafts an answer with citations; a qualified person decides whether the work may start.

introduction.title: What happens when a technician needs the official procedure?
introduction.context: Before working on a machine, a technician has to know what the written procedure actually requires — which switch is isolated, how tight a bolt goes, whether this job needs a second person. Those answers live across three kinds of document: federal safety regulation, the site's own written procedures, and the manual for that specific machine. Together that is thousands of pages. In practice people answer from memory or ask whoever is nearby, which is fine until it is not: a confident wrong answer about isolating a machine is how someone gets hurt.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one question: the technician asks in plain English, the question is checked for enough detail to look anything up, the system searches the indexed procedure library, a confidence policy decides whether the answer is genuinely in the documents, a draft answer is written with the citation for every claim, and a qualified person reads the cited passage before work starts. Exception paths reveal the refusal-and-escalation route and the corpus-curation loop that a wrong citation triggers.
introduction.startsWhen: A technician has a question about a job — a step, a setting, or a safety requirement — before starting the work.
introduction.endsWhen: A qualified person has verified the cited procedure and the work either proceeds or is escalated to someone who can answer.

decisions.label: Is the question specific enough to look anything up?
decisions.wrongCost: A vague question returns confident passages about the wrong machine entirely
decisions.testAnswer: No. What a lookup needs — the machine or system, the task, and what is actually being asked — is a short checklist known in advance.
decisions.why: "How tight should this be?" cannot be answered by any library. Asking for the missing piece up front costs seconds; a wrong-machine answer costs a lot more.
decisions.recommendation: Check for the machine, the task, and a question deterministically, and ask for exactly the missing piece rather than guessing at it.

decisions.label: Which passages in the library actually answer this question?
decisions.frequency: Every question that passes the completeness check
decisions.wrongCost: The technician is handed the right-sounding text from the wrong rulebook
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Technicians ask in shop language and the documents are written in legal language; matching the two is learned from examples, not from a list of keywords.
decisions.why: A technician asks about "locking out the press" and the regulation says "energy isolating device." A keyword search never connects them; a model trained on how language is used does.
decisions.recommendation: Return ranked passages with the citation attached to each one, keep a plain keyword search alongside as the honest comparison, and never let the model answer from its own memory.

data.summary: Three layers of public-domain documents: federal workplace safety regulation, one public facility's own written maintenance procedures, and the manual for a specific piece of equipment, plus plain-language safety booklets. Every regulation section arrives carrying its own official citation, so a right answer can be graded by exact citation match rather than by human judgment.
data.readiness: Public-domain sources fetched once at a pinned date and committed: 13 documents, roughly 400,000 words, every page carrying real selectable text
fields: Regulation section text with its official citation
Equipment manual procedures and torque tables
The section and paragraph labels each passage came from
Document version and the date it was fetched
data.risk: Different rulebooks repeat each other almost word for word. Adding one near-duplicate collection dropped the share of questions cited to the correct rule from 80 percent to 27 percent while the retrieved text barely changed — right words, wrong rule. The regulation also points at outside standards it does not contain, so for some questions the only correct answer is that the documents do not say.

method.output: Ranked passages with citations
method.technique: Similarity between meaning-based representations of the question and of section-bounded passages, measured against a plain keyword word-overlap search on the same questions; the meaning-based index won clearly on technician-phrased questions

metric.technical: Citation correctness — does the top passage carry the right rule number — rather than how similar the retrieved text looks, because the text can be right while the rule cited is wrong.
metric.business: Minutes saved per question against a technician searching the documents by hand, plus the share of questions that come back with a citation at all.
metric.baseline: A technician searching the PDFs by hand for about 12 minutes, or asking whoever is nearby

human.role: Qualified person — the named individual authorized to sign off this work
human.checkpoint: Reads the cited passage in the source document before any work begins. The assistant retrieves and drafts; it never authorizes work and never approves a lockout.
human.falsePositiveCost: A fluent answer citing the wrong rule sends a technician to a machine with the wrong procedure in hand — the failure this whole workflow exists to prevent.
human.falseNegativeCost: The assistant refuses a question the documents could have answered, and the technician spends about 12 minutes searching by hand instead (classroom assumption).

architecture: Passage splitter that carries section labels and citations
Meaning-based passage index with a keyword search for comparison
Question log and corpus curation review

decisions.label: Is the answer genuinely in the documents, or should the system refuse?
decisions.wrongCost: The system invents a number for a question the documents never answer
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the retrieval scores exist and the site has set how close a match must be, the branch is a comparison — though the line itself is chosen from measured results.
decisions.why: Refusing is a designed outcome here, not an error. The regulation regularly points at outside standards it does not contain, so the only correct answer to some questions is "this library does not say — ask someone who can." A system that always produces an answer will invent one.
decisions.recommendation: Version the confidence line, add an explicit rule for passages that reference a standard the library does not hold, and report the refusal rate and the wrong-refusal rate as headline numbers rather than hiding them.

decisions.label: Does the cited passage really say what the draft claims?
decisions.frequency: Every drafted answer, before work starts
decisions.wrongCost: Work begins under a procedure the document never contained
decisions.verdictLabel: Keep the human — safety owns it
decisions.testAnswer: More documents do not change who is accountable. A named qualified person has to stand behind the procedure before anyone touches the machine.
decisions.why: Fluency is not authority. An automatic self-check in the classroom build caught an invented torque figure but missed a pressure figure copied word for word from a wrong-but-retrieved passage — so "no unsupported claims" is not the same as "correct."
decisions.recommendation: Put the draft and the source passage side by side with the citation visible, require the qualified person to open the source before approving, and log the verdict either way.

decisions.label: Who answers a question the documents do not cover?
decisions.frequency: Every refusal and every failed verification
decisions.wrongCost: A refused question is quietly dropped and the technician proceeds on a guess
decisions.testAnswer: By definition the answer is not in the library, so no amount of retrieval reaches it. Someone with the authority and the outside standard has to answer.
decisions.why: A refusal only helps if it goes somewhere. Left as a dead end, it teaches technicians that the assistant is useless and pushes them straight back to answering from memory.
decisions.recommendation: Route every refusal to a named person with the question and the passages that were found, give the answer back to the technician, and log it so the library can be extended.

decisions.label: Is the library still pointing at the right rule?
decisions.frequency: Monthly, over a sample of logged questions
decisions.wrongCost: Retrieval keeps scoring well while citing rules that do not apply to this site
decisions.testAnswer: Judging whether two near-identical rulebooks both belong in one library is an editorial and legal call about which rules govern this site, not a pattern to be learned.
decisions.why: Curating the library beats tuning the model. Adding a near-duplicate collection in the classroom build cut correct citations from 80 percent to 27 percent while the retrieved text stayed almost the same, and the overall benchmark barely moved — the damage was invisible in the average.
decisions.recommendation: Review sampled questions with their citations each month, keep one authoritative copy of any duplicated rule, and re-measure citation correctness by document area rather than as one overall score.

title: One Week of Reorder Planning
subtitle: From the weekly sales file to a purchase order
learningObjective: Map a wholesaler's weekly replenishment as an operating process, turn a demand range into an order quantity priced against stockout and overstock costs, and keep the order itself with a planner.
throughline: The model produces a range, not a promise; the cost of being short versus the cost of being long picks the quantity inside that range; and a planner, never the system, places the order.

introduction.title: What happens in a wholesaler's weekly reorder planning?
introduction.context: This business sells gifts and homeware in bulk to shops, not to the public. It holds thousands of products in one warehouse, and every week it has to decide how many units of each one to buy from its suppliers. Order too few and a shop's order cannot be filled, so the sale goes to a competitor and may not come back. Order too many and the stock sits in the warehouse costing money until it is marked down. Nobody knows next week's demand. The planning team only knows what sold in the weeks before, and the whole job is deciding how to act on that.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one weekly planning cycle. The sales file closes on Sunday night, cancellations and non-product lines are removed, and the remaining order lines are totaled into one row per product per week. Products with too little history are set aside to be planned by hand. For the rest, a model produces a demand range for the coming week, a cost-based policy turns that range into an order quantity, and a planner approves, adjusts, or holds it. The purchase order goes to the supplier, the delivery is received, and next week's sell-through is recorded against what was ordered.

introduction.endsWhen: The purchase order is placed with the supplier and the delivery receipt is recorded against it.

decisions.label: Are these order lines usable sales of a real product?
decisions.wrongCost: Returns, postage charges and duplicate lines are counted as demand, so every forecast downstream is built on sales that never happened
decisions.testAnswer: No. A cancellation, a negative quantity, a zero price and a postage code are all recognizable by a fixed check that anyone can read.
decisions.why: In the classroom data roughly one line in fifty is a cancellation, tens of thousands of rows are exact duplicates, and codes like postage and bank charges look exactly like products until you filter them out.
decisions.recommendation: Drop cancellations, non-positive quantities and prices, duplicate rows and non-product codes with a documented rule, and log how many lines were removed each week so the removals stay visible.

decisions.label: Does this product have enough weeks of sales to be forecast at all?
decisions.wrongCost: A product with three weeks of history gets a confident-looking range that is really just noise, and somebody orders against it
decisions.testAnswer: No. How many weeks a product needs, and how many of them must have sales, is a requirement written down in advance.
decisions.why: Most of the catalog sells in bursts: the middle product in the classroom data has no sales at all in about two weeks out of three. Forecasting that is not hard, it is meaningless, and the honest answer is to say so rather than produce a number.
decisions.recommendation: Require a minimum number of weeks with sales inside the training window, and count those weeks on the training window only, never across the weeks the forecast will be tested on. Products that fail the check are sent to be planned by hand.

decisions.label: How many units of this product will sell next week, and how far either side of that could it plausibly land?
decisions.wrongCost: A number with no range around it gets ordered as if it were certain, and the warehouse ends the week either short or overstocked
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. How much a product sells next week depends on patterns in its own sales history that nobody can write down as a rule, and the width of the plausible range differs for every product.
decisions.why: This is the module's central idea. A forecast of 40 units is not a plan. A forecast of 40 units that could plausibly be 22 or 61 is a plan, because the order quantity depends on the width of that range, not on its center.
decisions.recommendation: Publish a demand range for the coming week with the interval and its nominal level shown together, and let the order policy and the planner decide what to do with it. Say what it claims: the forecast is not a promise, the interval is not a guarantee that demand will land inside it, and the system never places an order.

data.summary: A weekly demand panel built from a wholesaler's own order lines: one row per product per week, with the units sold in that week. Partial weeks at each end are dropped so every week is a full week. The cohort of steady sellers is chosen on the training window only, because counting sales weeks across the whole history would let the weeks used for testing pick the products.
data.owner: Sales operations, who own the order records
data.readiness: Prepared classroom dataset: a public wholesaler transaction log covering two years, cleaned and totaled into a weekly panel once at build time and committed as a small CSV
fields: Number of weeks with sales inside the training window
Weeks since the product first sold
data.risk: Most products sell in bursts, so a panel that looks complete is mostly zeros. The retailer is closed on Saturdays, which a daily model would learn as a fake weekly pattern and which is why the panel is weekly. Only about one year of usable history exists per product, so there is not enough to lean on a seasonal pattern. And selecting the steady-seller cohort across all weeks instead of the training window quietly leaks the test period into the setup.

method.output: A demand range, not a single number: a forecast of next week's units together with an interval around it at a stated level
method.technique: An eight-week moving average as the point forecast, with the interval built from that product's own past forecast errors as empirical quantiles, clipped at zero because demand cannot be negative. Compared against a seasonal-naive forecast, which is worse here than forecasting nothing at all because one year is not a season, and against quantile gradient boosting, which wins on average error but covers only three quarters of the weeks its interval promises and predicts negative demand on some rows.

metric.technical: Interval coverage measured against its nominal level, reported as a pair, alongside mean absolute error in units. Never a percentage error, which on products with zero-sales weeks divides by nearly nothing, inverts, and rates a forecast of zero as the best model in the room.
metric.business: Total cost of over- and under-ordering across the cohort, compared against ordering at the point forecast: on the frozen holdout the cost policy is about 9 percent cheaper at a 4:1 stockout-to-overstock ratio and about 28 percent cheaper at 9:1, and roughly break-even at 2:1.
metric.baseline: Order the point forecast with no range around it, or simply order what sold last week

human.checkpoint: The planner sees the proposed quantity, the range it came from, and the cost ratio that picked it, and then approves, adjusts, or holds the order. The system proposes a number and never places an order.
human.falsePositiveCost: Overstock: units sitting in the warehouse at a holding cost of about 10 percent of unit price per unit per week until they are marked down (classroom assumption).
human.falseNegativeCost: A stockout and a lost sale: the shop's order cannot be filled, the margin on those units is gone, and the shop may place its next order somewhere else.

architecture: Transaction log with cancellations and non-product lines removed
Training-window cohort selection for steady sellers
Per-product empirical residual quantiles for the interval
Newsvendor order-quantity policy with a configurable cost ratio
Sell-through log and weekly forecast review

decisions.label: Given the range, how many units should we actually order?
decisions.wrongCost: Ordering at the middle of the range treats a stockout and an overstock as if they cost the same, which they almost never do
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once the range exists and the business has priced a stockout against an overstock, the quantity is arithmetic anyone can check by hand.
decisions.why: The right quantity is not the average forecast. It is a point chosen inside the range by the critical ratio: the cost of being short divided by the cost of being short plus the cost of being long. At 4:1 that is the 80th percentile of the range; at 9:1 it is the 90th.
decisions.recommendation: Compute the critical ratio from the two costs, read the matching quantile out of the product's range, and version the cost ratio so a change to it is a visible business decision rather than a silent edit. Show the planner which percentile was used and what a different ratio would have ordered.

decisions.label: Should this proposed order be placed as it stands?
decisions.wrongCost: An order goes out against a promotion, a supplier problem or a one-off bulk sale that nobody told the model about
decisions.testAnswer: The panel knows what sold. It does not know that a customer is closing down, that a supplier has raised its minimum order, or that last week's spike was one shop's one-time buy.
decisions.why: The forecast is not a promise and the interval is not a guarantee. Somebody has to own the commitment of money to stock, and the system is explicitly not that somebody.
decisions.recommendation: Show the planner the quantity, the range, the cost ratio used and the product's recent weeks; let them approve, adjust or hold; and record the reason whenever they change the number, because those reasons are the fastest way to find what the model cannot see.

decisions.label: What do we order for a product that is brand new or being discontinued?
decisions.owner: Demand planner with the category buyer
decisions.frequency: Every product that fails the history check, every week
decisions.wrongCost: A new product is either not stocked at all or bought in bulk on a guess, and a discontinued line keeps being reordered
decisions.testAnswer: There is no history to learn from. A new product has no past weeks, and a discontinued one's past weeks describe a future that is not going to happen.
decisions.why: Producing a range from three weeks of data would look like a forecast and behave like a guess. Saying plainly that this product cannot be forecast yet is the more honest output, and it routes the decision to the person who knows the launch plan.
decisions.recommendation: Route these products to a hand-planned list with the buyer's launch or run-out plan attached, mark the quantity as hand-planned in the purchase order, and re-test the history check each week so a new product joins the forecast cohort as soon as it has earned enough weeks.

decisions.label: Is the cost policy still the right way to order this product?
decisions.owner: Weekly forecast review with the planning lead
decisions.frequency: Weekly, with the previous weeks' sell-through in hand
decisions.wrongCost: A policy that helps most of the range is left running on the products it actively hurts
decisions.testAnswer: The averages hide the losers. Deciding whether a product should be taken off the policy needs someone who knows whether it is declining, being replaced, or just having a quiet month.
decisions.why: On the frozen holdout the cost policy is cheaper for about three quarters of products at a 4:1 ratio and more expensive for the rest, and the losers are the declining sellers, where a range built from stronger past weeks keeps ordering for a demand that is going away. One product's costs rose by nearly five times.
decisions.recommendation: Review the products the policy made worse alongside the ones it helped, on the same page, every week. Take declining lines off the automatic quantity and hand-plan their run-out, and record the change rather than quietly widening the ratio for everyone.

title: One Page of Recommendation Slots
subtitle: From a shopper opening a page to a logged slot outcome
learningObjective: Map how a storefront fills its recommendation slots, judge a ranking model on products the shopper has never bought, and keep placement with the merchandisers who set the rules.
throughline: A ranking score measured on repeat purchases flatters a model that adds nothing; the honest measure is what the shopper has never bought, and the model ranks inside merchandiser rules rather than deciding what gets placed.

introduction.title: What happens when a storefront fills its recommendation slots?
introduction.context: This is the same wholesaler's online storefront. When a shop's buyer opens a product or category page, a strip near the bottom of the page has a fixed number of empty slots to fill with other products. Somebody has to decide what goes in them. Filling them with what this buyer already reorders is easy and looks successful, but it shows them nothing they did not already know about. Filling them with the same few bestsellers for everyone is also easy, and buries most of the catalog. And a good share of visitors have no purchase history at all, so there is nothing personal to work from.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one page view. The page requests items for its slots, the shopper's purchase history is looked up, and a check decides whether there is enough of it to personalize on. If there is, a ranking model scores products the shopper has not bought before; a slot policy sends already-bought items to a separate labeled strip; and merchandiser rules and exclusions filter what is left. The slots are filled, or the labeled fallback list is shown instead. What the shopper clicks and buys is logged, feeds the weekly model refresh, and is reviewed for whether the model is serving the whole catalog.
introduction.startsWhen: A shopper opens a product or category page that has recommendation slots on it.
introduction.endsWhen: The slots are filled, or the labeled fallback is shown, and the outcome of the slots is logged.

decisions.label: Does this shopper have enough purchase history to personalize on?
decisions.frequency: Every page view with recommendation slots
decisions.wrongCost: A shopper with one purchase gets a personal-looking list built from almost nothing, and it is labeled as if it were about them
decisions.testAnswer: No. How many past purchases are needed before a shopper can be personalized to is a threshold written down in advance and checked the same way every time.
decisions.why: About one shopper in five arrives with nothing usable, and every guest checkout is in that group. The model cannot rank for them at all: with no history its scores are the same for every product, so what looks like a ranking is really a tie broken at random.
decisions.recommendation: Check the count of prior purchases before calling the model, and route shoppers who fail the check to the fallback path rather than letting a model rank on an empty history.

decisions.label: Which products should be ranked highest for this shopper?
decisions.wrongCost: The slots fill with things the shopper would have bought anyway, or with the same bestsellers everyone sees, and the page teaches them nothing new
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Which products go together for which shoppers is learned from thousands of baskets and is not something a merchandiser can write out product by product across a catalog this size.
decisions.why: The pattern being used is that products bought by the same customers tend to suit the same customers. That similarity is learned from the transaction log, it changes as the catalog changes, and no fixed rule reproduces it. What it cannot do is decide placement.
decisions.recommendation: Return a ranked list of candidate products with their scores, and let the slot policy and the merchandiser rules decide what is actually shown. State the boundary plainly: an offline ranking score is not evidence of revenue, and the model ranks within merchandiser rules rather than deciding placement.

data.summary: The same wholesaler transaction log the demand forecast uses, reshaped instead into a customer by product matrix: one row per customer, one column per product, marked where that customer bought that product. It is about 98 percent empty. Training and testing are split by date, so the model is only ever built on purchases that happened before the ones it is judged on.
data.readiness: Prepared classroom dataset: the same committed transaction file as the forecasting case, pivoted once at build time into a customer by product matrix
fields: Whether that customer bought that product
Revenue on the line, used for the fallback list
Number of distinct products in the customer's history
data.risk: Almost a quarter of order lines have no customer id at all, so those shoppers can never be personalized to. A random train-test split would let purchases from the future teach the model about the past, which is why the split is by date. And the log records what the storefront chose to show as much as what shoppers wanted, so popular products are over-represented before any model is trained.

method.output: A ranked list of products the shopper has not bought before
method.technique: Item-item similarity: products are compared by which customers bought them, each product's similarity list is truncated to its nearest neighbors, and a shopper is scored by adding up the similarities from what they already own. Truncating to the nearest fifteen neighbors raised accuracy and catalog coverage at the same time and shrank the model artifact by more than two orders of magnitude. Compared against a popularity list, the recent-revenue fallback, and matrix factorization.

metric.technical: Hit rate in the top ten measured only on items the shopper has NOT bought before, because scoring on repeat purchases makes a worthless model look best: a list that simply re-shows what the customer already owns finishes first on the ordinary leaderboard and below a random list once repeats are masked. The same model, first and last, decided by what the analyst counts as a hit. Catalog coverage is printed next to every accuracy number.
metric.business: Incremental revenue from products the shopper had not bought before. The measured gain is small and must be reported as such: the best personalized model reaches about 3.5 percent of the available new-item revenue against about 2.8 percent with no personalization at all, a gap of under one percentage point, and that is an upper bound because an offline replay cannot show what a shopper would have done if shown something else.
metric.baseline: Fill the slots with what is popular right now, with no personalization at all

human.checkpoint: Merchandisers set the slot rules and the exclusion lists, and review what the slots actually served each week. The model ranks inside those rules; it does not decide placement, and it never overrides an exclusion.
human.falsePositiveCost: A slot spent on something irrelevant: the shopper ignores the strip, and repeated misses train them to stop looking at it at all.
human.falseNegativeCost: A product the shopper would have wanted never gets shown, which is invisible in the logs because nothing was ever displayed to click.

architecture: Transaction log shared with the demand forecasting case
Customer by product matrix built on a time-based split
Item-item similarity model truncated to the nearest neighbors
Slot eligibility and Buy it again split
Recent-revenue fallback list for shoppers with no history

decisions.label: Which ranked items are allowed to take a recommendation slot?
decisions.wrongCost: The slots fill with things the shopper already buys, the strip looks like it is working, and it adds nothing
decisions.testAnswer: No. Whether a shopper has bought a product before is a fact already in the record, and the number of slots is fixed, so the filtering is a lookup and a count.
decisions.why: Reordering is genuinely useful, but it is a different job from discovery and it must not be allowed to score as discovery. Keeping the two apart in the interface is what keeps them apart in the measurement.
decisions.recommendation: Fill the recommendation slots only with products the shopper has not bought before, and put already-bought items in a separate strip honestly labeled Buy it again. Report the two strips separately so neither one's numbers can be read as the other's.

decisions.label: What do we show a shopper we know nothing about?
decisions.frequency: Roughly one page view in five
decisions.wrongCost: A generic list is presented as personal, and the shopper is told the site knows them when it does not
decisions.testAnswer: No. With no history there is nothing to learn from. The fallback is a straightforward query over recent sales that anyone can read and check.
decisions.why: Cold start has no clever answer, and pretending otherwise is the failure. Measured here, ranking products by revenue over the last four weeks beats an all-time bestseller list, and both are honest as long as they are labeled for what they are.
decisions.recommendation: Show what is selling right now over a fixed recent window, label the strip Popular right now, and never label it Recommended for you. Log fallback impressions separately so their results are never mixed into the personalized numbers.

decisions.label: Should any of these products be kept out of the slots?
decisions.frequency: Rules set weekly, applied on every page view
decisions.wrongCost: A discontinued line, an out-of-stock item, or a product that must not sit beside another one ends up in a slot
decisions.testAnswer: The model only knows what has been bought together. It does not know what is being run out, what is legally restricted in a market, or what a supplier agreement requires.
decisions.why: This is where placement authority sits. The merchandisers own what appears on the page; the ranking model orders candidates within the boundaries they set.
decisions.recommendation: Keep exclusions and pinning rules in a list merchandisers own and can change without a model rebuild, apply them after ranking and never inside it, and log every time a rule removed an item so its cost is visible.

decisions.label: Is the model still serving more than the same handful of products?
decisions.frequency: Weekly, with the previous week's slot outcomes in hand
decisions.wrongCost: The strip quietly narrows to a few bestsellers, the accuracy numbers stay high, and most of the catalog is never seen by anyone
decisions.testAnswer: An accuracy score cannot tell you the model has stopped showing the catalog. Someone has to decide that reaching more products is worth a small loss of measured accuracy.
decisions.why: A pure popularity list scores respectably while ever showing about ten distinct products out of thousands, and the loop compounds: what gets shown gets bought, what gets bought trains next week's model. In a simulation of ten rounds of exposure, the top ten products went from about 2 percent of purchases to over 6 percent without a single new product entering the list.
decisions.recommendation: Report catalog coverage beside accuracy on every review, watch the share of slots taken by the top products week over week, and treat a narrowing strip as a decision for merchandisers to make deliberately rather than something the retraining loop does on its own.
